title: The Martyr
intro: Abd al-Rahim Mahmud wrote this poem during the great Palestinian revolt of 1936–1939, in which he fought, as Kamil al-Sawafiri records, and it appeared in the Beirut magazine al-Amali in its first year, in issue 21, which Izz al-Din al-Manasra dates to 1938. It opens with the poet's vow to carry his soul on his palm and fling it into danger, for either a life that gladdens a friend or a death that galls the enemy; he sees where he will fall in defence of his right and his land and hurries towards it, then pictures the martyr lying in the open, his blood dyeing the ground and scenting the wind, a smile of scorn for the world on his lips, and ends by refusing fear and humiliation and vowing to defend his land with the sword. Al-Sawafiri writes that the schoolboys and schoolgirls of Palestine who studied after the revolt of 1936 learned his rousing poems by heart, this one and “The Valiant People” foremost among them. In al-Risala in 1949, Muhammad Salim al-Rashdan told how, in the poet's last battle, as he ordered his men to fall back, one of them shouted, “Are you running away, you who said, ‘I will carry my soul on my palm’?”, and he leapt out into the gunfire repeating lines of this poem until he fell.

1.1.4.head: راحَة
1.1.4.meaning: Raha: the palm of the hand.

4.2.1-2.meaning: “Feared of side”: a man whose ground no one dares approach.

4.2.3-4.meaning: “Forbidden of hima”: the hima was land kept from others' grazing; his may not be trespassed on.

7.1.3.meaning: Dun: here “in defence of”, as in the Prophet's saying, “whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr”.

9.2.1.head: ناوَشَ
9.2.1.meaning: Snatch at it. The 1980 and 2009 editions have tanawashuhu, with the same sense.

10.1.3-4.meaning: “Lions of the sky”: birds of prey.

10.2.4.meaning: Al-Shara: a place known for its lions, said to lie by the Euphrates; “the lions of al-Shara” is a set phrase. The 1958 and 2009 editions have al-thara, “the soil”.

11.1.4.head: الأُرجُوان
11.1.4.meaning: Urjuwan: a deep red dye, purple.

11.2.3-4.meaning: The saba: the east wind, which blows from where the sun rises.

12.2.2.head: عُفار
12.2.2.meaning: Ufar: dust; the dictionaries give the word for dust as afar.

17.2.3-4.meaning: “Lord of refusal”: a man of the proudest spirit, who will not submit.

18.2.4.meaning: Laza: blazing fire; in the Quran, a name of Hell.

19.1.2.head: حِياض
19.1.2.meaning: Hiyad: watering troughs; here his land and all he protects.

19.2.4.meaning: Fata: a young man; also a man of courage and generosity.

translation: I will carry my soul on the palm of my hand
and fling it into the chasms of death.
1.sharh: He resolves to hold out his life on his open hand, ready to give it up at any moment, and to throw it where death lies waiting. To carry one's soul on one's palm is an Arabic way of saying that one is ready to die.

translation: Then either a life that gladdens a friend
or a death that galls the enemy.
2.sharh: Either outcome is a victory for him: a life of honour that makes his friends glad, or a death that infuriates his enemies, because they could not humble him.

translation: A noble soul has two ends in view:
to come down to the waters of death, or to win what it hopes for.
3.sharh: A noble spirit wants one of two things, death or the fulfilment of its hopes, and will settle for nothing in between. Going to meet death is pictured as coming down to water, and manaya, deaths, echoes muna, hopes.

translation: What is life (may I not live) if I am not
a man whose side is feared, whose ground is forbidden?
4.sharh: Life is worth nothing to him unless others fear him and nothing he protects can be violated. The aside “may I not live” is a curse he lays on himself should he ever accept less.

translation: When I speak, all the world listens to me,
and my words resound among mankind.
5.sharh: He boasts that his voice carries: when he speaks, everyone listens, and his words ring out among people. The line can also be read as one more condition of the life he would accept, after line 4.

translation: By your life, I can see where I will fall,
and still I quicken my steps towards it.
6.sharh: He swears that he sees the place of his death plainly ahead of him and, far from turning back, hurries towards it. He is not blind to the danger; he walks into it knowing what it is.

translation: I see that to fall defending my stolen right
and defending my land is the end I seek.
7.sharh: To die for the right that was taken from him and for his country is not a fate he puts up with but the very thing he seeks. The place of death he saw in line 6 now has its reason.

translation: The ring of swords is sweet to my ear,
and the flow of blood gladdens my soul,
8.sharh: What others dread in war, the clash of blades and the sight of blood, is a joy to him, because it means that the fight he longs for has come.

translation: and a body felled on the open plain,
with the hunting creatures of the wild snatching at it.
9.sharh: A fallen body gladdens him too: grammatically it is one more thing that delights him, after the flow of blood. From here the poem describes the martyr, stretched on the bare ground while birds and beasts of prey tear at him.

translation: A share of him goes to the lions of the sky,
a share to the lions of al-Shara.
10.sharh: His body is divided between the birds of prey, which the poet calls lions of the sky, and the lions of the earth. Only the strongest creatures feed on him, as if he keeps his dignity even in death.

translation: His blood clothed the earth in purple
and weighed the east wind down with scent.
11.sharh: His blood dyes the ground a deep red, as if dressing it in a robe, and its fragrance loads the breeze. The image probably recalls the Prophet's saying that a wound received in God's cause will come on the Day of Resurrection with the colour of blood and the scent of musk.

translation: It dusted his radiant brow,
but with a dust that adds to his beauty.
12.sharh: Dust settles on his shining forehead, yet it does not disfigure him; it only makes him more beautiful. To rub a man's face in the dust was to humiliate him, and the poet turns it into an ornament of the martyr.

translation: A smile showed on his lips,
and its meaning was scorn for this world.
13.sharh: Even in death he smiles, and the smile says that he despises the world he has left behind and leaves it without regret, as if he had seen something better.

translation: He fell asleep to dream the dream of eternity
and to delight in it in the sweetest visions.
14.sharh: Death is pictured as a peaceful sleep in which the martyr dreams of everlasting life. The idea likely echoes the Quran's words on those killed in God's cause, who are not dead but “alive with their Lord”.

translation: By your life, this is how men die;
whoever wants a noble death, here it is.
15.sharh: Turning back to his listener, he swears that this is the death worthy of men, and that anyone who seeks an honourable end need look no further.

translation: How then can I endure the plots of the spiteful?
How can I bear to be forced to suffer harm?
16.sharh: If such is the death of men, he cannot sit still under an enemy's malice or accept the humiliation forced on him. The questions are a refusal: he will bear neither.

translation: Fear, when life is cheap to me?
Humiliation, when I am the lord of pride?
17.sharh: Fear makes no sense in a man who cares nothing for his life, nor humiliation in one whose nature is to refuse it. Both questions throw the very idea back.

translation: With my heart I will strike at the faces of the enemy,
for my heart is iron and my fire a blaze.
18.sharh: His first weapon is his courage: he will hurl his own heart in the enemy's face, a heart as hard as iron and burning with a fierce fire.

translation: I will guard my watering places with the edge of the sword,
and my people will know that I am the man.
19.sharh: He will defend his land with the sword, and then his people will see that he is the one they can rely on. Guarding one's watering trough is an old Arabic image for protecting what a man holds sacred, as in Zuhayr's line that whoever does not defend his trough with his weapons will see it wrecked.
